notes.meaning: King Xerxes promotes Haman to the highest office in the empire, placing him above all other nobles as grand vizier. Calling him an Agagite links him to Agag, the ancient king of the Amalekites, who were long-standing enemies of God's people. This sudden rise to power sets the stage for a deadly conflict between Haman and the Jews.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Agagite was a Persian family or regional name, because Haman and his family have Persian names and the Amalekite kingdom had ended centuries earlier.

notes.meaning: The king orders all the royal gate officials to kneel and bow down to the earth before Haman. Mordecai flatly refuses to bow, because the Persian court demanded a kind of deep reverence that bordered on worship due only to God. For Mordecai, giving divine honor to any mortal man was a direct violation of his religious duty.

The palace officials at the gate notice Mordecai standing tall while everyone else falls prostrate. They question him directly to find out why he is breaking a clear royal order. Refusing an imperial command was dangerous and put his position and life at serious risk.

The officials urge Mordecai day after day to obey the command, but he refuses to change his mind. When he explains that he is a Jew and cannot give divine honor to a man, they report him to Haman to see if such a religious excuse will be permitted. His open confession makes his faith the central reason for his stand.

When Haman sees with his own eyes that Mordecai refuses to bow, he is consumed with uncontrollable anger. His vast pride cannot handle even a single person withholding the public honor he expects. Unchecked anger often blinds people to reason and leads to extreme cruelty.

Punishing Mordecai alone seems too small a revenge for Haman's wounded pride. Learning that Mordecai is a Jew, Haman decides to wipe out the entire Jewish population across the Persian Empire. His hatred expands from personal spite into a plan for total genocide.

In the spring of the king's twelfth year, Haman has pagan astrologers cast the lot, called the Pur, to pick a lucky date for the massacre. The lot falls on the twelfth month, nearly a full year away. While Haman relies on superstition, God quietly guides the outcome to provide ample time for His people to be saved.

Haman approaches King Xerxes with a misleading claim, craftily leaving out the name of the people he targets. He warns that a scattered group follows unique customs and ignores royal laws, making them a danger to the crown. By twisting the truth, he portrays their religious obedience to God as rebellion against the state.

Haman asks for a written royal order to destroy this people completely, promising to pay ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury. This astronomical sum was meant to make up for any lost tax revenue caused by their deaths. He likely planned to raise the funds by seizing the victims' property.

Xerxes takes off his signet ring and hands it to Haman without asking any questions about who will be killed. Giving the ring grants Haman full imperial authority to write and seal laws in the king's name. The king acts carelessly, placing absolute power over life and death into the hands of a bitter enemy.

The king tells Haman that he may keep the money and do whatever he pleases with the people. By waving off the payment, Xerxes presents himself as generous while blindly handing an entire nation over to slaughter. His lazy indifference leaves innocent people completely defenseless.

On the eve of Passover, royal scribes gather to draft the decree in every local script and language across the empire. The proclamation carries the full legal authority of Xerxes and is sealed with the royal signet ring. Writing to every governor ensures that the command will be enforced in every corner of the realm.

Royal couriers carry orders to every province to wipe out all Jews—men, women, and children—on a single day, the thirteenth of Adar. The decree also promises that anyone who kills them can seize all their goods as plunder. This offer of stolen wealth was designed to motivate the local populations to join the slaughter.

Copies of the edict are posted publicly in each province so that the general population can read it and prepare for that day. The public notice gives local citizens eleven months to arm themselves against their Jewish neighbors. It turns ordinary communities into waiting executioners.

The messengers ride out in haste, and the terrifying decree is announced in the fortress city of Susa. While the king and Haman sit down to drink wine, the ordinary residents of the capital are left confused and horrified by such senseless brutality. Evil leaders often celebrate while the people under their rule suffer deep distress.
